title: Sleeping on It
text: For centuries, people have advised one another to ‘sleep on’ a difficult decision, and modern research suggests that this folk wisdom may contain more than a grain of truth. During sleep, the brain does not simply switch off. Instead, it appears to replay and reorganise the experiences of the day, strengthening some memories while allowing others to fade.

In one study, volunteers who learned a list of word pairs in the evening and were tested the next morning remembered more than those who learned the same list in the morning and were tested after a day awake. Researchers caution, however, that the picture is far from simple. Different stages of sleep seem to serve different functions, and how much a person benefits may depend on the type of material learned. What is clear is that the habit of sacrificing sleep to cram for an exam may well be self-defeating.

questions.q: According to the text, what happens in the brain during sleep?
opts: It rests completely and stops processing information.
It sorts the day's memories, reinforcing some and letting others weaken.
It erases most memories of the day's events.
It creates new memories unrelated to what was experienced.
questions.why: Första stycket säger att hjärnan under sömnen ’replay and reorganise’ dagens upplevelser och stärker vissa minnen medan andra bleknar.

questions.q: What does the author imply about staying up late to study before an exam?
opts: It is the most efficient way to learn lists of words.
It is harmful only for certain types of material.
It is recommended by most sleep researchers.
It may undermine the very goal it is meant to achieve.
questions.why: Sista meningen kallar vanan att offra sömn för att plugga ’self-defeating’, alltså att den motverkar sitt eget syfte.

title: When Noon Was Local
text: Today it seems self-evident that clocks across a whole region should show the same time. Yet for most of human history, time was a strictly local affair. Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon at the moment the sun stood highest overhead. Because the sun's position shifts as one travels east or west, a town only a short distance away might keep a time that differed by several minutes. For communities whose inhabitants rarely travelled far, this patchwork caused little inconvenience.

The arrival of the railways changed everything. A timetable that listed departures in dozens of local times was not merely confusing; it was dangerous, since trains sharing a single track depended on precise scheduling to avoid collisions. In Britain, railway companies gradually adopted the time kept at Greenwich, and station clocks soon followed. Across North America, where distances were far greater, railway companies agreed in the 1880s to divide the continent into a handful of broad zones, each one hour apart.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Some critics regarded the new system as an arrogant attempt by private companies to dictate something as fundamental as the hour of the day. Newspapers carried complaints from citizens who felt that ‘God's time’, as determined by the sun, was being replaced by ‘railway time’, a mere commercial convenience. In some towns, public clocks were fitted with two minute hands, one showing local time and the other the time used by the trains.

Over the following decades, however, resistance faded. As telegraphs, factories and eventually radio broadcasts tied distant places ever more closely together, a shared standard became indispensable. Governments that had initially stood aside began to give the zones legal force. The episode is a reminder that conventions which now appear natural were once contested innovations, adopted not because they were obviously right but because a changing world made them useful.

questions.q: What is the main point of the text?
opts: Railway companies caused frequent accidents by ignoring local time.
Local solar time was more accurate than the zone system that replaced it.
Standardised time, now taken for granted, arose from practical needs and was at first resisted.
Governments were the driving force behind the introduction of time zones.
questions.why: Texten beskriver hur järnvägen gjorde gemensam tid nödvändig, att den möttes av motstånd, och sista stycket sammanfattar att konventionen infördes för att den var användbar.

questions.q: Why does the author mention clocks with two minute hands?
opts: To show how some communities tried to accommodate both systems of time.
To illustrate how inaccurate public clocks were in the nineteenth century.
To explain how railway companies enforced their new timetables.
To suggest that local time was quickly abandoned everywhere.
questions.why: I tredje stycket visade klockorna både lokal tid och järnvägstid, ett sätt att hantera båda systemen under övergången när alla inte accepterade förändringen.

questions.q: The phrase ‘stood aside’ in the final paragraph is closest in meaning to
opts: resigned from office.
remained uninvolved.
actively opposed the change.
took a leading role.
questions.why: Regeringarna hade först ’stood aside’ men började sedan ge zonerna laglig kraft, alltså hade de tidigare hållit sig utanför frågan.

title: Borrowed Words
text: Every language borrows. English, for instance, has absorbed vast numbers of words from Norse, French and Latin, and it continues to import terms from languages around the world. Purists sometimes see this as a sign of decline, warning that a language flooded with foreign vocabulary will lose its character. Linguists tend to take a calmer view. Borrowed words are rarely adopted unchanged: they are typically adapted to the sounds and grammar of their new home, acquiring native-looking plurals and endings until speakers forget they were ever foreign. A word's origin, in other words, says little about whether it belongs. Moreover, borrowing tends to fill gaps rather than displace existing vocabulary, supplying names for new objects, ideas and practices. Seen in this light, a language's willingness to borrow is less a symptom of weakness than evidence of its vitality and of its speakers' contact with the wider world.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the linguists' view as presented in the text?
opts: Borrowed words should be approved by official bodies before use.
Most borrowed words replace native words that already existed.
Languages that borrow heavily risk losing their identity.
Borrowing is a normal process that tends to enrich a language.
questions.why: Lingvisterna har en ’calmer view’: lånord anpassas, fyller luckor i stället för att tränga undan ord, och lån visar språkets ’vitality’.

title: Cities That Hold the Heat
text: On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can remain several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside long after sunset. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island, has been recognised for well over a century, but it has attracted renewed attention as heatwaves become more frequent and more intense.

The causes are well understood. Asphalt, concrete and brick absorb solar energy during the day and release it slowly at night. Tall buildings trap heat between them and reduce the wind that might otherwise carry it away. Meanwhile, the vegetation that cools rural areas through evaporation has largely been paved over. Add the waste heat from vehicles, air conditioners and industry, and the result is a landscape that functions rather like a storage heater.

The consequences are not merely a matter of discomfort. Prolonged heat places strain on the human body, and the risks fall most heavily on the elderly, the chronically ill and those living in poorly insulated housing. Because poorer neighbourhoods often have fewer trees and parks, the burden of urban heat is frequently distributed unequally, a point that has made the issue as much a question of social justice as of climate.

Fortunately, many remedies are relatively simple. Planting street trees, creating green roofs and replacing dark surfaces with lighter, more reflective materials can all lower local temperatures. Some cities have begun to map their hottest districts in detail so that such measures can be targeted where they are most needed. None of these interventions will halt global warming, but they may determine how bearable a warming world proves to be for those who live in its cities.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a cause of the urban heat island?
opts: Moisture rising from rivers and canals in the city.
Building materials that store heat and release it at night.
Tall buildings that block the wind.
The loss of vegetation that cools through evaporation.
questions.why: Andra stycket nämner byggmaterial, höga hus som stoppar vinden, förlorad växtlighet och spillvärme, men inget om fukt från floder eller kanaler.

questions.q: Why does the author describe urban heat as ‘a question of social justice’?
opts: Because wealthy residents use more air conditioning than others.
Because city governments refuse to plant trees in central areas.
Because its effects fall hardest on vulnerable and poorer groups.
Because rural residents are unfairly blamed for rising temperatures.
questions.why: Tredje stycket säger att riskerna drabbar äldre, sjuka och fattigare områden med färre träd och parker hårdast, alltså ojämlikt fördelat.

questions.q: Which best describes the author's attitude to the remedies discussed in the final paragraph?
opts: Dismissive, since they cannot stop global warming.
Cautiously positive, while acknowledging their limits.
Enthusiastic, believing they will solve the climate problem.
Neutral, offering no judgement of their value.
questions.why: Författaren skriver ’Fortunately’ och kallar åtgärderna enkla och värdefulla, men påpekar att de inte stoppar den globala uppvärmningen.

title: The Curious Power of Sugar Pills
text: Few findings in medicine are as puzzling, or as frequently misunderstood, as the placebo effect. In clinical trials, patients who receive an inactive substance, such as a sugar pill or a saline injection, often report genuine improvements in their symptoms. For decades, this response was treated mainly as a nuisance: a source of noise that researchers had to subtract in order to measure the ‘real’ effect of a new drug. Only relatively recently has the placebo response itself become an object of serious scientific study.

One reason for the change is the growing recognition that the effect is not imaginary in any simple sense. Brain-imaging studies have shown that, in some patients, taking a placebo painkiller is accompanied by measurable changes in brain regions associated with the processing of pain, and in some cases by the release of the body's own pain-relieving chemicals. The expectation of relief, it seems, can set in motion physiological processes that partly deliver it.

Expectation, however, is only part of the story. The context in which treatment is given appears to matter a great deal. Some research suggests that the colour, size and even the price of a pill can influence how well patients believe it works. Perhaps more significantly, the quality of the relationship between patient and practitioner seems to shape outcomes. In one study, patients who received a placebo treatment from a warm and attentive clinician reported greater improvement than those who received the same treatment from a brisk and distant one. Such findings suggest that what we call the placebo effect might be better described as the effect of the whole ritual of care.

The most surprising recent development concerns so-called open-label placebos. Conventional wisdom held that a placebo could only work if the patient was deceived into thinking it was real medicine. Yet several small trials have found that some patients, particularly those with chronic conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome or lower back pain, report improvements even when they are told openly that the pills they are taking contain no active ingredient. Researchers are still debating why this should be. One possibility is that the act of taking a pill regularly, with all its associations of being cared for, triggers a conditioned response learned over a lifetime of medical treatment.

It is important not to overstate what placebos can do. The effect tends to be strongest for subjective symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue, and there is little convincing evidence that a placebo can shrink a tumour or cure an infection. Enthusiasts who suggest otherwise risk encouraging patients to abandon treatments that work. There is also a darker counterpart to the placebo, known as the nocebo effect: when patients are warned about possible side effects, some begin to experience them, even if they have been given an inactive substance.

For doctors, these findings present both an opportunity and a dilemma. Deceiving patients is widely regarded as unethical, which is one reason open-label placebos have attracted such interest. More broadly, however, the research suggests that ordinary clinical practice could be improved without any deception at all. Taking time to listen, explaining a treatment clearly and expressing realistic confidence in it may all enhance the benefit that patients derive from real medicine. In this sense, the study of the placebo has less to do with sugar pills than with the long-neglected question of how the experience of being treated contributes to healing.

questions.q: According to the text, how did researchers traditionally regard the placebo response?
opts: As the most promising area of medical research.
As proof that most drugs have no real effect.
As an ethical problem that should be hidden from patients.
As an obstacle to measuring the true effect of drugs.
questions.why: Första stycket säger att placeboresponsen länge sågs som ’a nuisance’, brus som måste räknas bort för att mäta läkemedlets verkliga effekt.

questions.q: What does the study involving the warm and attentive clinician suggest?
opts: Placebos work only when given by experienced doctors.
The way care is delivered can influence how much patients improve.
Patients prefer clinicians who spend little time with them.
Warm clinicians tend to prescribe more effective medicines.
questions.why: Tredje stycket visar att samma behandling gav större förbättring hos en varm läkare, vilket tyder på att hela ’ritual of care’ påverkar resultatet.

questions.q: The author mentions the nocebo effect in order to
opts: show that expectations can also produce harmful effects.
argue that patients should not be told about side effects.
prove that open-label placebos are dangerous.
explain why placebos cannot cure infections.
questions.why: Femte stycket kallar nocebo placebons ’darker counterpart’: varningar om biverkningar kan ge biverkningar, alltså kan förväntningar också skada.

questions.q: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
opts: Placebos should replace conventional drugs for chronic pain.
Open-label placebos have been proven to work through conditioning.
Placebo research can improve medical practice without deceiving patients.
The placebo effect is purely psychological and has no physical basis.
questions.why: Sista stycket säger att vanlig vård kan förbättras ’without any deception at all’ genom att lyssna, förklara och visa realistisk tilltro.

title: The Price of Free
text: Many of the digital services people use most often, from search engines and social media platforms to email accounts, cost nothing to use. Or so it appears. Economists have long pointed out that when a product is offered free of charge, the user is frequently not the customer but part of what is being sold. The genuine customers are advertisers, who pay for access to the attention and data that users supply.

This arrangement has obvious benefits. It has made powerful tools available to anyone with an internet connection, regardless of income. A student in a remote village can, in principle, use the same search engine as a professor at a wealthy university. Few would wish to return to a world in which such services were available only to those who could pay for them.

Yet the model also creates incentives that are not always aligned with users' interests. If a company's revenue depends on how long people spend on its platform, it has every reason to design features that are hard to put down, whether or not this time is well spent. Critics argue that endlessly scrolling feeds, autoplaying videos and a constant stream of notifications are not accidental features but the predictable outcome of a business model built on capturing attention.

Proposed remedies vary. Some advocate subscription models, in which users pay directly and the company has less reason to maximise engagement. Others favour stricter regulation of how personal data may be collected and used. Still others place their hopes in education, arguing that users who understand how these platforms make money will be better equipped to use them on their own terms. Each approach has drawbacks: subscriptions may exclude poorer users, regulation can be slow and clumsy, and education places the burden on individuals rather than on the companies whose design choices are at issue.

questions.q: What does the author mean by saying that the user ‘is frequently not the customer but part of what is being sold’?
opts: Users are secretly charged for services they believe are free.
Users often resell digital services to other people.
Users' attention and data are what companies sell to advertisers.
Users have no legal rights as consumers of free services.
questions.why: Nästa mening förklarar att de egentliga kunderna är annonsörer som betalar för tillgång till användarnas uppmärksamhet och data.

questions.q: Why does the author mention a student in a remote village?
opts: To illustrate how free services give wide access regardless of income.
To criticise the unequal quality of education in rural areas.
To show that free services are used mostly by young people.
To argue that professors should pay for digital services.
questions.why: Exemplet står i stycket om fördelarna: verktygen är tillgängliga för alla med internet ’regardless of income’.

questions.q: What is the author's view of the proposed remedies?
opts: Subscription models are clearly the best solution.
Regulation is the only approach likely to succeed.
Education is preferable because it respects individual freedom.
Each has weaknesses, so none offers a simple solution.
questions.why: Sista meningen säger ’Each approach has drawbacks’ och nämner en nackdel för var och en av prenumeration, reglering och utbildning.

title: Whose Heritage?
text: Museums in Europe and North America hold vast numbers of objects that were acquired during the colonial era, some through purchase or exchange, others through looting or coercion. In recent years, governments and communities in the countries of origin have increasingly asked for these objects to be returned. Some museums have agreed, handing back items that had been displayed far from home for well over a century.

Others have resisted, arguing that their collections allow visitors from around the world to see the achievements of many cultures side by side, or that the circumstances of an acquisition can no longer be established with certainty. Supporters of return respond that the question is not where an object can be seen by the greatest number of people, but who has the right to decide. For them, an artefact taken by force remains a reminder of injustice for as long as it stays where it is, however carefully it is preserved.

questions.q: Which argument is used by museums that resist returning objects?
opts: The objects were all bought legally and fairly.
Their collections let visitors see many cultures in one place.
The countries of origin lack suitable museums.
The objects would be damaged during transport.
questions.why: Andra stycket säger att museerna menar att samlingarna låter besökare se många kulturers prestationer ’side by side’.

questions.q: According to supporters of return, what is the central issue?
opts: How carefully the objects are preserved.
How many people are able to see the objects.
How much the objects are worth financially.
Who has the right to decide over the objects.
questions.why: Förespråkarna säger att frågan inte är var flest kan se föremålet ’but who has the right to decide’.

title: Counting Birds, Building Science
text: Every winter, in many countries, thousands of volunteers spend an hour or so watching their gardens, local parks or balconies and recording the birds they see. Individually, their observations might seem trivial. Combined, they form one of the most valuable sources of information that ecologists possess about how bird populations are changing over time.

Projects of this kind are examples of what has become known as citizen science: research in which members of the public, most of them without formal scientific training, help to collect or analyse data. The approach is not new, since amateur naturalists have contributed to science for centuries, but digital technology has transformed its scale. Smartphone apps allow observations to be submitted instantly, complete with photographs and precise locations, and online platforms enable volunteers to classify images of distant galaxies or transcribe handwritten weather records from previous centuries.

Professional scientists were initially sceptical. Data gathered by amateurs, they worried, would be riddled with errors: misidentified species, inconsistent methods, and a tendency to report the unusual while ignoring the commonplace. These concerns were not unfounded. However, researchers have developed statistical techniques to account for such biases, and studies comparing volunteer and expert observations have often found the differences to be smaller than expected. Where errors do occur, the sheer volume of data can compensate for some of the imprecision of individual records.

The benefits are not confined to science. Participants frequently report that taking part has made them more attentive to their surroundings and more concerned about the environment. In this sense, citizen science may serve as a bridge between researchers and the public at a time when trust in expertise cannot be taken for granted. Its most enthusiastic advocates go further, arguing that it represents nothing less than a democratisation of knowledge itself.

questions.q: According to the text, what has changed most about citizen science in recent years?
opts: Its scale, thanks to digital technology.
Its focus, which has shifted from birds to astronomy.
Its participants, who now mostly have scientific training.
Its acceptance, which is now universal among scientists.
questions.why: Andra stycket säger att metoden inte är ny men att ’digital technology has transformed its scale’, med appar och onlineplattformar.

questions.q: What does the sentence ‘These concerns were not unfounded’ (paragraph 3) suggest?
opts: The scientists' worries were entirely mistaken.
The concerns had never been properly investigated.
There was some justification for the scientists' worries.
The worries were raised mainly by the volunteers themselves.
questions.why: ’Not unfounded’ betyder att farhågorna hade viss grund; texten fortsätter med ’However’ och beskriver hur man hanterar felen.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the author's attitude to the claim in the final sentence?
opts: The author regards it as the main conclusion of the research.
The author presents it as a bolder view than the author necessarily shares.
The author considers it completely absurd.
The author believes scientists invented it to attract volunteers.
questions.why: Författaren tillskriver påståendet ’its most enthusiastic advocates’ som ’go further’, vilket visar distans utan att avfärda det.

title: Too Much to Read
text: Complaints about information overload are usually treated as a symptom of the digital age. We are told that the internet, with its endless stream of articles, messages and videos, has overwhelmed our capacity to pay attention, and that previous generations, with their limited supply of books and newspapers, enjoyed a calmer relationship with knowledge. Historians, however, have pointed out that such anxieties are far from new.

When printing with movable type spread across Europe in the second half of the fifteenth century, the number of books in circulation grew at a pace that contemporaries found astonishing. Texts that had once existed in a handful of hand-copied manuscripts could now be produced in hundreds or thousands of identical copies. For many, this was cause for celebration. Knowledge that had been the preserve of monasteries and wealthy collectors became, at least potentially, available to a far wider public.

Others were less enthusiastic. Within a few generations, scholars were lamenting that there were simply too many books for anyone to read, and that the good were being drowned out by the bad. Some worried that cheap printing allowed error and heresy to spread as easily as truth. Others feared that readers, faced with such abundance, would skim rather than study, accumulating fragments of knowledge without ever mastering a subject. The parallels with present-day concerns about the internet are difficult to miss.

What is perhaps most interesting is not the complaints themselves but how people responded to them. Faced with an unmanageable quantity of text, scholars and printers developed an array of tools for finding their way through it. Alphabetical indexes, tables of contents and page numbers, all of which are now so familiar as to be invisible, became increasingly common features of printed books. Compilers produced vast reference works, such as encyclopaedias, bibliographies and anthologies of excerpts, designed to spare readers the trouble of consulting the original sources. Individual readers, meanwhile, refined elaborate systems of note-taking, copying useful passages into notebooks organised under thematic headings so that they could be retrieved later.

These innovations did not eliminate the problem of abundance; arguably, they never could. What they did was to change the nature of reading itself. Alongside the slow, repeated reading of a small number of revered texts, there emerged a different mode: selective, purposeful consultation, in which the reader moved quickly through a book in search of particular information. Critics saw this as a decline in seriousness. Defenders might have replied that it was simply an adaptation to new circumstances, and that the ability to find and evaluate information was itself a form of learning.

The comparison with our own time should not be pushed too far. The volume of information available today is vastly greater, and it reaches us not only through deliberate searches but through feeds designed to hold our attention. Nevertheless, the history of early print offers a useful corrective to the assumption that the present is uniquely bewildering. It suggests that societies faced with an explosion of information do not simply suffer; they invent. The search engines, filters and recommendation systems of today may be seen as descendants of the humble index, and the debates about their effects on our minds are part of a conversation that has been going on for more than five hundred years.

questions.q: What is the main argument of the text?
opts: Worries about information overload have historical precedents, and people have responded by inventing new tools.
The printing press caused more harm to learning than the internet has.
Modern readers are less serious than readers in the age of manuscripts.
Reference works made it unnecessary for scholars to read original sources.
questions.why: Texten visar att oro för informationsöverflöd fanns redan efter boktryckarkonsten och att samhällen ’do not simply suffer; they invent’, t.ex. register och uppslagsverk.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a concern of early critics of printing?
opts: Good books would be drowned out by bad ones.
Error and heresy would spread easily.
Readers would skim instead of studying properly.
Scribes who copied books by hand would lose their jobs.
questions.why: Tredje stycket nämner för många böcker, spridning av fel och kätteri samt ytlig läsning, men ingenting om att avskrivare skulle bli arbetslösa.

questions.q: In paragraph 5, what does ‘this’ in ‘Critics saw this as a decline in seriousness’ refer to?
opts: The slow, repeated reading of revered texts.
The selective, purposeful consultation of books.
The invention of the alphabetical index.
The spread of printing to a wider public.
questions.why: Meningen före beskriver det nya läsättet, ’selective, purposeful consultation’, och det är detta kritikerna såg som mindre seriöst.

questions.q: Why does the author say that the comparison with today ‘should not be pushed too far’?
opts: Because historians disagree about the effects of printing.
Because early print had no influence on modern technology.
Because today's information is far greater in volume and reaches us differently.
Because people in the past did not actually complain about too many books.
questions.why: Sista stycket förklarar att informationsmängden i dag är ’vastly greater’ och når oss via flöden designade för att fånga uppmärksamheten.

title: Too Many Choices?
text: It seems obvious that having more options is better than having fewer. If a shop offers twenty kinds of jam rather than five, customers are more likely to find one that suits their taste exactly. Yet a well-known line of psychological research has challenged this intuition, suggesting that an abundance of choice can sometimes leave people less satisfied, or even unable to decide at all.

In one frequently cited experiment, shoppers who encountered a large display of products were more likely to stop and look, but less likely to make a purchase, than those who encountered a small display. Similar patterns were reported in other settings, from the selection of pension plans to the choice of essay topics. The explanation offered was that comparing many options is mentally taxing, and that the more alternatives we reject, the more we worry that one of them might have been better.

The idea, often called choice overload, proved enormously appealing. It was taken up by business consultants and popular writers, and it seemed to offer a scientific basis for the vague sense that modern consumer life had become exhausting. However, later attempts to reproduce the original findings produced a more complicated picture. Some studies found the effect; others found none; a few even found that larger assortments made people more likely to choose. When researchers pooled the results of many experiments, the average effect appeared to be close to zero.

This does not mean that choice overload is a myth. Rather, it seems to depend heavily on circumstances. The effect is more likely to appear when options are difficult to compare, when people have no clear preferences in advance, and when they feel under pressure to make the right decision. In other situations, a wide selection is welcomed. The story of choice overload thus illustrates a broader lesson about psychological research: striking findings from single experiments deserve a degree of caution until it is clear when, and for whom, they hold.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why might a large number of options reduce satisfaction?
opts: Large displays make products look cheaper.
People distrust shops that offer too much.
Comparing many options is demanding, and rejected alternatives cause doubt.
Most of the options are usually of poor quality.
questions.why: Andra stycket förklarar att jämförelser är ’mentally taxing’ och att ju fler alternativ vi väljer bort, desto mer oroar vi oss för att ett var bättre.

questions.q: What did later attempts to reproduce the original findings show?
opts: The results varied considerably from study to study.
Choice overload was confirmed in almost every case.
The original experiment had been deliberately falsified.
Larger assortments always made people more likely to buy.
questions.why: Tredje stycket: vissa studier fann effekten, andra inte, några fann motsatsen, och sammantaget var medeleffekten nära noll.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the final paragraph?
opts: To reject the idea of choice overload completely.
To advise shops to reduce the number of products they offer.
To criticise popular writers for misunderstanding psychology.
To argue that the effect depends on context and to draw a wider lesson about research.
questions.why: Sista stycket säger att effekten ’depend heavily on circumstances’ och avslutar med en allmän lärdom om att vara försiktig med enskilda experiment.

title: A Mind in Eight Arms
text: Octopuses have long fascinated biologists, not least because their intelligence seems to have evolved along a path entirely separate from our own. Their last common ancestor with vertebrates was a simple worm-like creature that lived hundreds of millions of years ago, yet octopuses can solve puzzles, open jars and escape from supposedly secure tanks. Strikingly, a large proportion of their neurons are located not in the brain but in the arms, which appear able to respond to their surroundings with a degree of independence. This has led some researchers to suggest that octopuses may offer something close to a glimpse of how a mind might be organised on another planet. Their intelligence is all the more puzzling given that most species live only a year or two and spend much of that time alone, conditions that are usually thought to work against the evolution of complex cognition.

questions.q: Why does the author find octopus intelligence ‘all the more puzzling’?
opts: Because octopuses have fewer neurons than most vertebrates.
Because octopuses live short and largely solitary lives.
Because octopuses are closely related to humans.
Because octopuses rarely solve problems in the wild.
questions.why: Sista meningen säger att de flesta arter lever bara ett eller två år och mest ensamma, förhållanden som anses motverka komplex intelligens.

title: Working Less, Achieving More?
text: The five-day working week is a relatively modern invention. For much of the nineteenth century, factory workers in industrialising countries routinely laboured six days a week, often for ten hours or more a day. The two-day weekend became widespread only in the twentieth century, after long campaigns by trade unions and, in some cases, the realisation by employers that rested workers were more productive. It is perhaps not surprising, then, that some now ask whether the next step might be a four-day week.

In recent years, companies and public bodies in several countries have experimented with the idea, typically reducing working hours without reducing pay. Reports from many of these trials have been encouraging. Participating organisations have often stated that productivity remained stable, while employees described lower levels of stress and burnout and a better balance between work and private life. A number of firms chose to continue with the shorter week after the trial period ended.

Sceptics urge caution in interpreting these results. Organisations that volunteer for such trials are likely to be those already well suited to them, and the enthusiasm of participants who know they are being observed may inflate the benefits, at least in the short term. Moreover, the model is easier to apply in some sectors than in others. An office whose work can be reorganised around fewer and more focused meetings is in a very different position from a hospital ward or a bus company, where a reduction in hours may simply mean hiring more staff.

None of this means the idea should be dismissed. It does suggest, however, that the four-day week is unlikely to arrive as a single, universal reform. A more probable outcome is a gradual and uneven spread, in which shorter hours become common in some industries long before they are feasible in others, much as the weekend itself once did.

questions.q: Why does the author begin with the history of the working week?
opts: To argue that working conditions have barely changed.
To praise employers for introducing the weekend voluntarily.
To criticise trade unions for demanding too much.
To show that norms about working time have changed before and could change again.
questions.why: Första stycket visar att femdagarsveckan är en sen uppfinning och drar slutsatsen att det inte är förvånande att man nu frågar om fyradagarsvecka.

questions.q: Which concern raised by sceptics is mentioned in the text?
opts: Organisations that volunteer for trials may be unusually well suited to them.
Employees in the trials reported higher levels of stress.
Productivity fell sharply in most trials.
Shorter weeks are illegal in many countries.
questions.why: Tredje stycket säger att organisationer som anmäler sig frivilligt sannolikt redan passar väl för modellen, vilket kan ge för positiva resultat.

questions.q: What does the author predict about the four-day week?
opts: It will soon be introduced by law in most countries.
It will be abandoned once the trials end.
It will spread gradually and unevenly across different sectors.
It will be adopted first by hospitals and transport companies.
questions.why: Sista stycket förutspår ’a gradual and uneven spread’ där vissa branscher går före andra, precis som helgen en gång gjorde.

title: Bringing Back the Wolves
text: In the mid-1990s, after an absence of roughly seventy years, grey wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in the United States. The animals had been deliberately exterminated there in the early twentieth century, at a time when predators were widely regarded as vermin to be eliminated for the sake of livestock and game. Their return was controversial among local ranchers, but for many conservationists it was a landmark: an attempt not merely to protect a species but to restore a missing piece of an ecosystem.

In the years that followed, a remarkable story took shape. According to this account, the presence of wolves changed the behaviour of elk, the park's most numerous large herbivores. No longer able to graze undisturbed along riverbanks, the elk moved more often and avoided places where they might be ambushed. Freed from constant browsing, young willow and aspen trees began to recover. Their return in turn benefited songbirds and beavers, whose dams altered the flow of streams and created new wetland habitats. The wolves, it seemed, had set off a chain of effects reaching all the way down to the shape of the rivers themselves.

This kind of chain reaction, in which a predator at the top of a food web influences plants and animals several steps below it, is known as a trophic cascade. The Yellowstone story became perhaps the most famous illustration of the concept, retold in textbooks, documentaries and countless online videos. It also became a powerful argument for what is now called rewilding: the idea that conservation should aim to restore natural processes, including the presence of large predators, rather than simply preserving isolated fragments of habitat.

More recently, however, a number of ecologists have questioned whether the story is quite as tidy as it is often presented. They point out that wolves were not the only factor affecting elk numbers during this period. Human hunting outside the park, growing populations of other predators such as bears and cougars, and a series of dry years all played a role. Some studies have found that the recovery of trees has been patchy, strong in some locations and barely noticeable in others. In places where beavers had disappeared, streams had cut deeper channels and the water table had dropped, the return of wolves alone may not be enough to reverse decades of change.

None of these researchers claim that wolves have had no effect. The debate is rather about the size of that effect and about the danger of reducing a complex system to a simple narrative. Ecosystems, they argue, rarely respond to a single intervention in a straightforward way; outcomes depend on history, climate and the actions of many species, including our own. A story in which one charismatic animal ‘saves’ a landscape is appealing precisely because it is simple, but its very simplicity may create unrealistic expectations about what reintroductions elsewhere can achieve.

The disagreement has practical implications. Across Europe, wolves have been returning to regions from which they had long been absent, in most cases spreading on their own rather than being deliberately released. Their arrival has provoked fierce debate between those who welcome them as a symbol of ecological recovery and those, particularly farmers, who must cope with the loss of livestock. If the benefits of predators are exaggerated, public support may erode when the promised transformations fail to materialise; if they are underestimated, opportunities for restoration may be missed. Perhaps the most valuable lesson of Yellowstone, then, is not that wolves can work miracles but that ecological recovery is a slow, uncertain process that demands patience, careful observation and a willingness to revise cherished stories in the light of evidence.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, how did the presence of wolves supposedly help trees to recover?
opts: The wolves ate the insects that damaged young trees.
The elk changed their behaviour and browsed less along riverbanks.
The wolves' dens created new wetland habitats.
Park managers planted trees to provide cover for the wolves.
questions.why: Andra stycket säger att älgarna (elk) inte längre kunde beta ostört vid flodbankarna, rörde sig mer, och att unga träd då kunde återhämta sig.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph 4?
opts: To explain why wolves were exterminated in the first place.
To describe how beavers build their dams.
To argue that wolves should be removed from Yellowstone again.
To present evidence that complicates the popular account.
questions.why: Fjärde stycket inleds med att ekologer ifrågasätter om berättelsen är så ’tidy’ och nämner andra faktorer som jakt, andra rovdjur och torka.

questions.q: The word ‘tidy’ in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
opts: clean.
small.
simple and neat.
well documented.
questions.why: Kritikerna menar att verkligheten är mer komplicerad än den enkla berättelsen; ’tidy’ betyder här prydligt enkel, vilket stycke 5 bekräftar med ’simple narrative’.

questions.q: Which best describes the author's position in the final paragraph?
opts: Balanced, stressing patience and a willingness to revise beliefs in light of evidence.
Strongly opposed to the return of wolves in Europe.
Convinced that wolves can restore any damaged ecosystem.
Indifferent to the practical consequences of the debate.
questions.why: Författaren väger både överdrivna och underskattade fördelar och avslutar med att återhämtning kräver tålamod och vilja att revidera berättelser utifrån evidens.

title: Lost and Found in Translation
text: For most of the twentieth century, the dream of a machine that could translate between languages seemed perpetually just out of reach. Early attempts, beginning in the years after the Second World War, relied on sets of hand-written rules: dictionaries that matched words in one language with words in another, combined with grammatical instructions for rearranging them. The results were often comic. Language, it turned out, was far too irregular, and far too dependent on context, to be captured by any manageable set of rules.

A shift came when researchers stopped trying to teach computers the rules of language and instead let them learn from examples. By analysing enormous collections of texts that had already been translated by humans, among which parliamentary proceedings and international agreements were particularly useful, statistical systems calculated which words and phrases were most likely to correspond to one another. Translation became less a matter of understanding than of probability. The quality improved noticeably, though the output still often read as stilted and fragmentary.

The more dramatic leap came with systems based on artificial neural networks, which spread rapidly from the middle of the 2010s. Rather than translating phrase by phrase, these systems process whole sentences, and increasingly whole passages, producing text that is often fluent enough to pass for human writing. For many everyday purposes, such as understanding the gist of a foreign news article, reading a menu or exchanging messages with a colleague abroad, they are now entirely adequate, and they are used by vast numbers of people every day.

Fluency, however, can be deceptive. Because the output reads smoothly, errors are harder to spot than they were when machine translation was obviously clumsy. A system may confidently produce a sentence that is grammatically perfect but subtly, or even seriously, wrong in meaning. It may struggle with irony, wordplay and cultural references, or reproduce biases present in the texts it learned from, for example by assuming that a doctor is male and a nurse female when translating from a language that does not mark gender. Performance also varies greatly between languages. Systems tend to work best for languages with large amounts of digital text available and considerably worse for the thousands of languages for which such resources are scarce.

These limitations matter most where the stakes are highest. In legal, medical and diplomatic contexts, a small error can have serious consequences, and most institutions still insist on human oversight. The work of professional translators has accordingly begun to change. Many now spend a growing share of their time on what is known as post-editing: reviewing and correcting machine-generated drafts rather than translating from scratch. Some welcome the tools as a way to work faster; others complain that the task is less creative and less well paid, and that it risks reducing a skilled craft to a form of proofreading.

Literary translation presents perhaps the most interesting case. Translating a novel or a poem involves countless decisions about rhythm, tone and connotation, as well as judgements about how much of the original's strangeness to preserve for a new audience. Such decisions are not simply a matter of finding equivalent words; they reflect an interpretation of the work as a whole. Whether machines will ever make them well is an open question. What seems clear is that the long-standing assumption that translation is a mechanical task, a matter of swapping one set of words for another, has been thoroughly overturned, ironically by the very machines that were once expected to confirm it.

questions.q: Why did early rule-based translation systems largely fail?
opts: Language proved too irregular and context-dependent to capture in rules.
Computers at the time could not store dictionaries.
Researchers lacked access to translated texts.
Governments stopped funding translation research after the war.
questions.why: Första stycket säger att språket var ’far too irregular, and far too dependent on context’ för att fångas i en hanterbar uppsättning regler.

questions.q: According to the text, why can the fluency of modern systems be a problem?
opts: It makes translations too long to read quickly.
It causes users to stop learning foreign languages.
It makes errors harder to detect.
It makes the texts sound old-fashioned.
questions.why: Fjärde stycket: eftersom texten flyter väl är fel ’harder to spot’ än när maskinöversättning var uppenbart klumpig.

questions.q: What does the text suggest about post-editing?
opts: It has completely replaced traditional translation.
Professional translators are divided in their views of it.
It is used mainly for literary translation.
It is better paid than translating from scratch.
questions.why: Femte stycket säger att vissa välkomnar verktygen för att arbeta snabbare medan andra klagar på att arbetet blir mindre kreativt och sämre betalt.

questions.q: What is the irony referred to in the final sentence?
opts: Machines now translate poetry better than novels.
Translators who opposed machines now depend on them.
Statistical methods turned out to be better than neural networks.
Machines expected to show that translation is mechanical have instead revealed its complexity.
questions.why: Antagandet att översättning är mekaniskt har vederlagts ’by the very machines that were once expected to confirm it’ – det är ironin.

title: The Underground Exchange
text: Beneath the floor of a forest lies a dense web of fungal threads that wrap around, and in some cases penetrate, the roots of trees. This partnership, known as mycorrhiza, is ancient and, in most cases, mutually beneficial: the fungi draw sugars from the trees, and in return they deliver water and mineral nutrients that roots alone would struggle to reach.

In recent years, the idea that these networks allow trees to ‘talk’ to one another, warning neighbours of insect attacks or nursing their own seedlings, has captured the public imagination. Some ecologists, however, have grown uneasy. They point out that many of the most striking claims rest on a handful of field studies, some of which have proved difficult to replicate, and that evidence of resources moving between trees does not by itself show that the transfer is purposeful. The fungi, after all, may simply be serving their own interests.

questions.q: What does the text say about the relationship between the fungi and the trees?
opts: The fungi exploit the trees without giving anything back.
Both partners generally gain something from it.
It is a recent development in the history of forests.
The trees depend on it only for their supply of sugar.
questions.why: Texten kallar samarbetet ’in most cases, mutually beneficial’: svamparna får socker och träden får vatten och näring.

questions.q: What concern do some ecologists raise?
opts: Fungal networks are harmful to young trees.
Field studies of forests are too expensive to carry out.
Trees communicate mainly through their leaves, not their roots.
Popular accounts have gone further than the evidence justifies.
questions.why: Ekologerna påpekar att de mest uppseendeväckande påståendena vilar på få studier som är svåra att upprepa, och att resursflöden inte bevisar avsikt.

title: The Box That Shrank the World
text: Few inventions of the twentieth century look less remarkable than the shipping container. It is, after all, little more than a steel box of standard dimensions. Yet economic historians increasingly argue that this unglamorous object did as much to reshape global trade as any trade agreement negotiated during the same period.

Before containers came into widespread use in the 1960s, loading a ship was a slow and labour-intensive affair. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels and crates of every conceivable size, and gangs of dockworkers had to stow each item by hand. A vessel might spend as long in port as it did at sea, and theft and breakage were so common that they were treated as an ordinary cost of doing business. Transport was frequently the largest single expense in moving a product from factory to customer, which meant that for many goods it simply did not pay to manufacture them far from where they would be sold.

Standardisation changed this arithmetic. Because every container had the same dimensions and fittings, it could be lifted by crane from a lorry or train directly onto a ship and back again without its contents ever being touched. Loading times fell from days to hours, insurance costs dropped, and ports were redesigned around enormous cranes and storage yards rather than warehouses and workers.

The consequences were not uniformly welcome. Long-established port districts in many cities fell into decline as shipping moved to new, purpose-built terminals, often far from the old city centres, and tens of thousands of dock jobs disappeared. At the same time, the dramatic fall in transport costs made it feasible for companies to split production across several countries, assembling components made in one place into products finished in another. In this sense, the humble box laid some of the groundwork for the global supply chains that are now taken for granted.

questions.q: What point does the writer make in the first paragraph?
opts: The container was hailed as a remarkable invention when it was introduced.
Trade agreements were more important than the container for global trade.
The container's influence is out of proportion to its simple appearance.
Economic historians have overestimated the role of the container.
questions.why: Första stycket kontrasterar den ’unglamorous’ stållådan med att den förändrade världshandeln lika mycket som vilket handelsavtal som helst.

questions.q: According to the text, why were many goods produced close to their markets before containers were introduced?
opts: Moving them over long distances was too expensive to be worthwhile.
Dockworkers refused to handle goods from distant countries.
Insurance companies would not cover goods transported by sea.
Factories were not yet able to produce goods in large quantities.
questions.why: Andra stycket säger att transporten ofta var den största kostnaden, så det ’did not pay’ att tillverka varor långt från där de såldes.

questions.q: Which of the following does the text present as a negative consequence of containerisation?
opts: Goods were damaged more often during loading.
Traditional harbour areas lost much of their economic role.
Ships had to spend longer periods in port.
Companies were forced to concentrate production in one country.
questions.why: Sista stycket säger att gamla hamnkvarter ’fell into decline’ när sjöfarten flyttade till nya terminaler och att många hamnjobb försvann.

title: Paths of Desire
text: Anyone who has crossed a park has probably noticed them: narrow trails of worn grass that cut across lawns, ignoring the paved walkways laid out by designers. Planners call these informal routes ‘desire lines’, and they have long been treated as a nuisance, to be blocked with fences or hedges. A growing number of architects, however, regard them as ___ information. A desire line records, in a way no survey could, where people actually want to go rather than where someone assumed they would go.

Some universities have even delayed paving new campuses until students have had a year to tread their own paths, and only then laid concrete along the routes that emerged. The approach is not without its critics, who note that the shortest route is not always the safest, but it reflects a wider shift towards designing around observed behaviour.

questions.q: Which word best fits the gap (___) in the text?
opts: misleading
outdated
confidential
valuable
questions.why: Meningen inleds med ’however’ som kontrast mot synen på stigarna som ’a nuisance’, och nästa mening förklarar att de visar var folk faktiskt vill gå – alltså värdefull information.

questions.q: Why have some universities waited before paving their campuses?
opts: To lay paths along the routes people actually choose to walk.
To save money until enough students had enrolled.
To protect the grass from being damaged by students.
To give critics time to assess the safety of the routes.
questions.why: Texten säger att man väntade ett år tills studenterna trampat upp egna stigar och sedan lade betong längs de vägar som uppstått.

title: Reading the Rings
text: Every spring and summer, a tree in a temperate climate adds a new layer of wood beneath its bark. Growth is rapid early in the season, producing pale, wide cells, and slows as autumn approaches, producing darker, denser wood. The result, visible in any cross-section of a trunk, is a series of concentric rings, one for each year of the tree's life.

That much has been understood for centuries. What turned ring-counting into a science was the realisation that the width of the rings is not constant. In a wet year a tree grows generously; in a dry one it may barely grow at all. Because trees of the same species in the same region respond to the same weather, they share a recognisable sequence of wide and narrow rings, much like a bar code. In the early twentieth century, an American astronomer who had originally hoped to find evidence of solar cycles in tree growth developed methods for matching these patterns across different trees.

The technique, known as dendrochronology, proved far more useful than its founder could have anticipated. By overlapping the patterns from living trees with those from old timbers preserved in buildings, bogs and archaeological sites, researchers have built unbroken chronologies stretching back thousands of years in some regions. A wooden beam from a medieval church can now often be dated to the very year in which the tree was felled.

The rings also serve as a natural archive of past climate. Since they record conditions year by year, they allow scientists to reconstruct droughts and cold spells long before any thermometer existed, and to place recent changes in a much longer context. Yet the method has its limits: in tropical regions, where the seasons are less pronounced, many trees do not form clear annual rings at all.

questions.q: What makes it possible to date old pieces of wood precisely?
opts: Pale and dark wood can be distinguished under a microscope.
Old timbers contain more rings than living trees do.
Variations in ring width form patterns that can be matched between trees.
Medieval builders recorded the year in which each tree was felled.
questions.why: Andra och tredje stycket förklarar att ringarnas bredd varierar med vädret och bildar en ’bar code’ som kan matchas mellan levande träd och gammalt virke.

questions.q: What does the text suggest about the founder of dendrochronology?
opts: He was primarily interested in dating medieval buildings.
He was originally pursuing a different scientific question.
He doubted that tree rings could reveal anything about climate.
He developed the method while working in tropical regions.
questions.why: Texten säger att astronomen från början hoppades hitta belägg för solcykler, och att metoden blev ’far more useful than its founder could have anticipated’.

title: Two Languages, One Brain
text: For a time, it seemed that speaking two languages offered benefits far beyond the obvious ones. A series of influential studies in the early 2000s reported that bilingual children and adults outperformed monolinguals on tasks that required them to ignore distractions or switch rapidly between rules. The explanation offered was intuitive: because both languages are always active in a bilingual mind, the speaker is constantly practising the suppression of one in favour of the other.

More recent work has been less obliging. Several large studies have failed to find any consistent advantage, and some researchers suspect that the early findings owed something to small samples and to the tendency of journals to publish striking results rather than null ones. None of this, it should be stressed, undermines the value of learning a language; it simply suggests that the case for doing so should rest on communication rather than on mental gymnastics.

questions.q: What does the text say about more recent research?
opts: It has largely failed to confirm the earlier findings.
It has shown that bilingualism harms concentration.
It has confirmed the advantage, but only in children.
It has been rejected by most academic journals.
questions.why: Andra stycket säger att flera stora studier ’have failed to find any consistent advantage’.

questions.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
opts: Learning a second language is of little real value.
Bilingual people should train their minds in other ways too.
Journals should stop publishing research on bilingualism.
Learning a language is best justified by its use for communication.
questions.why: Sista meningen säger att argumentet för språkinlärning bör bygga på ’communication rather than on mental gymnastics’.

title: Borrowing Beyond Books
text: Public libraries have always been more than warehouses for books, but some are now stretching the definition further than ever. Alongside novels and reference works, a growing number lend out power drills, sewing machines, camping tents, telescopes and even musical instruments. The logic behind these so-called libraries of things is straightforward. Many household tools are used only a handful of times in their lifetime; the average electric drill, it is often claimed, runs for a mere fifteen minutes or so before being consigned to a cupboard. Sharing such items, advocates argue, saves money, reduces waste and frees up space in cramped homes.

The practical obstacles, however, are considerable. Unlike a book, a lawnmower can break, injure its user or come back caked in mud. Libraries have had to work out how to check items for safety, who is liable if something goes wrong and how to ___ the cost of repairs without discouraging the very people the service is meant to help. Some charge a small fee; others rely on volunteers and donations.

Supporters insist that the benefits go beyond economics. Borrowers often stay to ask advice, swap tips or sign up for repair workshops, and librarians report that the tool shelf has brought in people who had not set foot in the building for years. Whether such schemes can survive once the initial enthusiasm fades remains to be seen, but they suggest that the library's traditional mission of providing shared access to resources can be extended well beyond the printed page.

questions.q: Which word best fits the gap (___) in the text?
opts: ignore
cover
inflate
conceal
questions.why: Nästa mening förklarar hur biblioteken betalar reparationerna (avgift, frivilliga, gåvor) – de måste alltså täcka kostnaden.

questions.q: What additional benefit do supporters of these schemes point to?
opts: They allow libraries to reduce their spending on books.
They make it unnecessary for people to own any tools.
They bring people into the library and encourage contact between them.
They train librarians to repair household equipment.
questions.why: Tredje stycket säger att låntagare stannar för att fråga och utbyta tips och att verktygshyllan lockat tillbaka folk som inte besökt biblioteket på åratal.

questions.q: What is the writer's view of the long-term future of libraries of things?
opts: It is uncertain whether they will last.
They are certain to replace traditional book lending.
They will fail because of the safety risks involved.
They will survive only if they become commercial businesses.
questions.why: Texten säger att det ’remains to be seen’ om satsningarna överlever när den första entusiasmen lagt sig.

title: Notes in the Margins
text: Medieval manuscripts were copied by hand, often over many months, and the scribes who produced them were expected to remain invisible. Their task was to reproduce a text faithfully, not to comment on it. Yet in the margins of surviving manuscripts, historians have found a surprising number of personal remarks. Copyists complain that the ink is thin, that the parchment is rough, that their hands are cold or that the light is failing. One notes with evident relief that the work is finally finished and asks for a drink. Such scribbles are rarely more than a line long, but scholars value them highly. In a period from which few ordinary voices survive, they offer a rare glimpse of the daily experience of the people whose labour preserved much of what we know about the past.

questions.q: Why, according to the text, do scholars value the scribes' marginal notes?
opts: They correct errors in the main texts of the manuscripts.
They show that scribes often disagreed with what they copied.
They help historians date the manuscripts precisely.
They shed light on the lives of people who are otherwise seldom heard.
questions.why: Sista meningen säger att anteckningarna ger en sällsynt inblick i vardagen för vanliga människor i en tid då ’few ordinary voices survive’.

title: The Right to Repair
text: When a smartphone screen cracks or a washing machine stops spinning, many owners discover that fixing the problem is surprisingly difficult. Spare parts may be unavailable to anyone outside the manufacturer's network, repair manuals are often kept confidential, and some devices are designed in ways that make them almost impossible to open without damaging them. In some cases, software checks prevent a replacement part from working unless it has been authorised by the original maker. Faced with a repair bill that approaches the price of a new product, consumers frequently give up and buy a replacement.

A movement known as ‘right to repair’ argues that this state of affairs is both wasteful and unfair. Its supporters, who range from environmental groups to farmers frustrated at being unable to service their own tractors, want manufacturers to be required to make parts, tools and information available to independent repairers and to owners themselves. Electronic waste, they point out, is one of the fastest-growing waste streams in the world, and extending the life of products is among the simplest ways of reducing it.

Manufacturers have not always welcomed these demands. They argue that amateur repairs may compromise safety, that opening up technical information could expose devices to security risks, and that their own authorised networks guarantee a standard of work that independent workshops cannot match. Critics respond that such concerns, while not entirely groundless, are conveniently aligned with the companies' interest in controlling the lucrative market for repairs and in encouraging customers to upgrade.

In recent years, legislators in several countries have begun to side, at least partly, with the campaigners. New rules in some places require that certain appliances be designed so that they can be dismantled with ordinary tools and that spare parts remain available for a set number of years after a model is discontinued. It is too early to say how far such measures will change the habits of consumers, but they mark a notable shift in where the burden of responsibility is thought to lie.

questions.q: According to the first paragraph, why do consumers often buy a new product instead of having the old one repaired?
opts: New products are usually of higher quality.
Independent repairers refuse to work on modern devices.
A repair may cost almost as much as a new product.
Manufacturers offer discounts to customers who upgrade.
questions.why: Första stycket avslutas med att reparationskostnaden ’approaches the price of a new product’, så konsumenterna ger upp.

questions.q: How do the critics mentioned in the third paragraph view the manufacturers' objections?
opts: As partly valid but also convenient for the companies' business.
As entirely without foundation.
As a sincere concern for customer safety and nothing else.
As proof that independent repair is dangerous.
questions.why: Kritikerna säger att farhågorna är ’not entirely groundless’ men passar bekvämt med företagens intresse av att kontrollera reparationsmarknaden.

questions.q: What does the final paragraph indicate?
opts: Consumers have already changed their buying habits.
Some lawmakers have begun to place new obligations on manufacturers.
The right-to-repair movement has achieved all of its aims.
Manufacturers have voluntarily published their repair manuals.
questions.why: Sista stycket beskriver nya regler som kräver att apparater går att ta isär och att reservdelar finns kvar i ett visst antal år.

title: Finding the Way Home
text: Homing pigeons released hundreds of kilometres from their lofts, in places they have never seen, will usually find their way back within hours. How they do so has puzzled scientists for well over a century, and the answer appears to be that they rely not on a single sense but on several. Experiments suggest that pigeons use the position of the sun as a compass, adjusting for the time of day by means of an internal clock. On overcast days, when the sun is hidden, they seem able to fall back on the earth's magnetic field.

Closer to home, familiar landmarks such as roads, rivers and coastlines take on greater importance, and some birds have been tracked following motorways for long stretches. More controversially, a number of researchers argue that smell plays a role, ___ the birds may build up a kind of map from the odours carried on the wind. The debate continues, but most agree that the system's strength lies in its redundancy.

questions.q: Which expression best fits the gap (___) in the text?
opts: suggesting that
despite the fact that
on condition that
as long as
questions.why: Ledet efter luckan förklarar vad forskarnas tes om luktsinnet innebär (en karta av dofter), så ’suggesting that’ är det enda som ger rätt logiskt samband.

questions.q: What is meant by the final sentence of the text?
opts: Pigeons rely mainly on their sense of smell.
Scientists have finally agreed on how pigeons navigate.
Pigeons can still navigate when one source of information is unavailable.
Pigeons often waste time by checking the same information twice.
questions.why: ’Redundancy’ betyder att flera system överlappar; texten visar t.ex. att duvorna använder magnetfältet när solen är dold.

title: After the Plague
text: The Black Death, which swept across Europe in the middle of the fourteenth century, killed perhaps a third or more of the continent's population within a few years. Its immediate effects were catastrophic, but historians have long noted a paradoxical consequence for many of those who survived. With so many labourers dead, land was plentiful and workers were scarce, and peasants who had previously had little bargaining power found that they could demand higher wages or move in search of better terms.

Landowners and authorities did not accept this shift quietly. In England, laws were passed within a few years attempting to fix wages at their pre-plague levels and to restrict the movement of workers. Such measures proved difficult to enforce, and resentment over them is often counted among the causes of the major revolt that broke out in 1381. Over the longer term, the bonds that had tied many peasants to a particular lord gradually loosened.

questions.q: What paradoxical consequence of the Black Death does the text describe?
opts: Landowners became wealthier than ever before.
The population grew faster than it had before the plague.
Peasants lost the right to move to other areas.
Many survivors found their economic position improved.
questions.why: Första stycket säger att arbetskraftsbristen gav bönderna förhandlingsstyrka att kräva högre löner eller flytta till bättre villkor.

questions.q: How did the authorities in England respond?
opts: They encouraged peasants to move to the towns.
They tried to keep wages down by passing laws.
They raised wages to prevent a revolt.
They gave land to peasants who had survived.
questions.why: Andra stycket säger att lagar antogs för att låsa lönerna på nivån före pesten och begränsa arbetarnas rörlighet.

title: When Night Disappears
text: For most of the history of life on earth, night has been reliably dark. Within little more than a century, that has changed across much of the planet. Street lamps, illuminated buildings and advertising screens now cast a glow that can be seen from space, and in many cities the night sky is so bright that only a handful of stars remain visible.

The human cost of this change, in the form of disrupted sleep, has received considerable attention. Less well known is its effect on other species. Many nocturnal insects are drawn towards artificial lights, around which they may circle until they die of exhaustion or are picked off by predators. Since moths and other night-flying insects pollinate a significant number of plants, researchers have begun to ask whether lighting contributes to the widely reported decline in insect populations. Studies in which areas were experimentally lit have recorded fewer visits by nocturnal pollinators to flowers and, in some cases, reduced seed production.

Unlike many environmental problems, light pollution could in principle be reversed almost overnight: when a lamp is switched off, its effect ends at once. In practice, the solutions are rarely so simple. Lighting is associated with safety, and proposals to dim streets tend to meet with resistance. More promising, perhaps, are measures that reduce harm without plunging cities into darkness, such as shielding lamps so that light is directed downwards, using warmer colours that attract fewer insects and dimming lights in the small hours when few people are about.

questions.q: What do the experiments mentioned in the second paragraph indicate?
opts: Artificial light may interfere with the pollination of plants.
Insects avoid areas that are brightly lit.
Artificial light improves seed production in some plants.
Predators are less active in lit areas.
questions.why: Försöken med upplysta områden visade färre besök av nattliga pollinerare och ibland minskad fröproduktion.

questions.q: According to the text, what distinguishes light pollution from many other environmental problems?
opts: It affects humans more than other species.
It has existed for most of the history of life.
Its effects cease as soon as the source is removed.
It can only be seen from space.
questions.why: Tredje stycket säger att ljusföroreningar i princip kan upphävas direkt: ’when a lamp is switched off, its effect ends at once’.

questions.q: Which approach does the writer seem to consider most realistic?
opts: Switching off all street lighting at night.
Persuading people that dark streets are safe.
Moving people out of brightly lit city centres.
Changing how and when lights are used rather than removing them.
questions.why: Författaren kallar åtgärder som minskar skadan ’without plunging cities into darkness’ – avskärmning, varmare färger, nattdämpning – ’more promising’.

title: The Invention of the Average Man
text: In the 1830s, the Belgian astronomer and statistician Adolphe Quetelet began applying to human beings the mathematical methods that astronomers used to deal with errors in their observations. Measuring the chests of thousands of soldiers, he found that the results clustered around a central value, with fewer and fewer cases the further one moved from it. To Quetelet, this pattern was deeply significant. He proposed that the average represented a kind of ideal, an ‘average man’ towards which nature aimed, and that individual variations were, in effect, errors.

The idea proved enormously influential. It encouraged governments to gather statistics on crime, marriage, illness and death, and it helped to establish the conviction that society itself could be studied scientifically, with regularities as reliable as those of the physical world. Quetelet was struck, for instance, by how steady the annual number of crimes in a country remained, as though a certain level of wrongdoing were built into the society rather than being the free choice of individuals.

Later thinkers took a more critical view. If the average is treated as the norm, they pointed out, then deviation from it can easily come to be seen as abnormal or even defective, a conclusion with troubling implications when applied to human beings. Moreover, an average can describe a population without describing any actual member of it. A frequently repeated, though possibly embellished, story tells of an attempt to design aircraft cockpits around the average dimensions of pilots, only to find that hardly any pilot came close to the average on all measurements at once.
None of this means that averages are useless; they remain indispensable tools. But Quetelet's legacy is a reminder that a statistical summary is not the same as a person.

questions.q: How did Quetelet interpret differences between individuals?
opts: As evidence that the average had no real meaning.
As departures from an ideal that nature was aiming at.
As the result of mistakes in his own measurements.
As proof that each person freely chooses how to live.
questions.why: Första stycket säger att Quetelet såg medelvärdet som ett ideal ’towards which nature aimed’ och de individuella variationerna som ’errors’.

questions.q: What point is the story about aircraft cockpits used to illustrate?
opts: Pilots were unusually large compared with other people.
Aircraft designers ignored statistical data.
An average may not correspond to any real individual.
Averages are the most reliable basis for design.
questions.why: Berättelsen följer direkt på påståendet att ett medelvärde kan beskriva en population ’without describing any actual member of it’.
